newsitem.title: CHINA: China postpones launch of Apstar 2R satellite.
newsitem.headline: China postpones launch of Apstar 2R satellite.

text.p: China Aerospace Industry Co has delayed the launch of the Apstar 2R satellite to September from late August due to questions over control of the orbiter after its launch, industry sources said on Wednesday.

The decision to delay the launch date was taken at a meeting in Beijing on Tuesday between the satellite's owner, Beijing-controlled Hong Kong firm APT Satellite Holdings Ltd, and Chinese state launcher China Aerospace Industry Co, the sources said.
"The launch will not be in August," a Hong Kong-based industry source said. "The new target window is September 5."
Another industry source said the launch date could be September 10.
China Aerospace was still on schedule to launch the Philippines Mabuhay communications satellite around August 10 aboard one of China's new generation Long March 3B rockets, the sources said.
The Apstar 2R had been due to be sent aloft later that month, also on a Long March 3B rocket, the sources said.

The Apstar launch date had long been in doubt because 30-45 days were usually required between launches and there had also been problems concerning the control of the satellite after its launch, the first source said.
"There was a scheduling conflict with the contractor who controls the satellite between when the rocket dispenses it and its arrival in its final orbit," he said.
However APT denied any change in the satellite's schedule.
"The launch date will not be postponed," an APT spokesman told Reuters. "It will still be in late August."
Officials of China Aerospace declined to comment.
China is relying on the successful launch of the Mabuhay and Apstar 2R satellites to restore confidence in its space industry after a series of disasters since 1995.
In January 1995, a Long March 2E rocket carrying the original Apstar 2 satellite blew up shortly after blast-off, killing a family of six in a rain of fiery debris.

Then came the February 1996 loss of the first 3B and its U.S.-built Intelsat 708 satellite payload, followed in August by the failure of a Long March 3 rocket to put its Chinasat-7 orbiter into the proper orbit.
